summary: Makes the point that the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) does not tie Internet number resources to the real-world identity of whoever holds them. The document states that RPKI does not associate resources with the identity of their holder, correcting a common misunderstanding. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: A key card proves you may open a door, not who you really are. RPKI works that way: it shows who holds a block of addresses, not their real name.

questions: what does rpki certify about internet number resources
what does the i in rpki stand for
can i sign documents with rpki keys
what is an rpki certificate for
subtitle: Why RPKI certificates prove who may speak for addresses and AS numbers, never who a company really is.

tldr.problem: Some people want to use RPKI private keys to sign arbitrary documents as the holder of Internet number resources, expecting the signature to vouch for the document and the signer's identity.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC states that RPKI is for authorization only: a certificate lets its key speak for specific resources, and RPKI credentials MUST NOT be used to authenticate real-world documents or transactions.
tldr.outcome: The RPKI keeps its narrow job of verifying delegations of Internet number resources, and anyone needing real-world identity must use some formal external authentication of authority.

facts.label: Core rule
facts.value: RPKI credentials MUST NOT authenticate real-world documents or transactions

today: RFC 9255 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2022. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Misunderstanding
sections.content:
The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), described in RFC 6480, represents the allocation hierarchy of IP address space and Autonomous System (AS) numbers. Together these are called Internet Number Resources (INRs). Since its first deployment the RPKI has grown to include related data such as Router Keying for BGPsec.

A public key implies a private key. The RPKI gives strong authority to the current holder of INRs, and some people want to use the private keys to sign arbitrary documents as the INR 'holder'. They expect the signature to attest that the document is authentic. The RFC says this is inappropriate: the certificate is only an authorization to speak for the explicitly identified INRs.
sections.plainLanguage: Some people wanted to use a key that proves who controls some internet addresses to sign any paper. But that key was never made to say who the signer really is.

sections.title: The Bait and Sushi Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example. Bill's Bait and Sushi (BB&S) could use the key that shows it holds its AS in the RPKI to sign a Letter of Authorization (LOA) letting another party rack and stack hardware that BB&S owns. The RFC says that while this may be technically possible, it is neither appropriate nor meaningful.

The 'I' in RPKI stands for "Infrastructure" (Resource Public Key Infrastructure), not for "Identity". The RPKI does not associate INRs with the real-world holders of those INRs.
sections.plainLanguage: A fish-and-sushi shop could sign a note with its address key, but that does not prove the note is real. The 'I' stands for infrastructure, not identity.

sections.title: RPKI Is for Authorization
sections.content:
The RPKI was designed to sign certificates for use inside the RPKI itself and to generate Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) for use in routing. Its design intentionally precluded attesting to real-world identity because, among other issues, that would expose the Certification Authority (CA) to liability. The RFC adds that trying to do so would end in a world of complexity with no proof of termination.

Registries such as the Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) provide the mapping from INR to real-world identity through WHOIS and similar services, and they claim to be authoritative for the INRs they allocate.

The core rule is stated with a requirement word: RPKI-based credentials of INRs MUST NOT be used to authenticate real-world documents or transactions. That might be done with some formal external authentication of authority allowing an otherwise anonymous INR holder to authenticate a document or transaction. Given such external verification, RPKI credentials add no authenticity.
sections.plainLanguage: The address keys were built to answer 'who may announce these addresses?' and nothing else. If you want to know who someone really is, ask the registry or use some other proof.

sections.title: Why the Key Does Not Mean the Holder
sections.content:
The RFC lists several reasons. RFC 6480 says explicitly that certificates do not attest to the identity of the subject, and the CPS template in RFC 7382 says the Subject name in each certificate SHOULD NOT be meaningful.

  • Normally the INR holder does not hold the private key; the CA does. The holder only has a business relationship with the CA, so schemes such as Resource Tagged Attestations and Signed Checklists must go to great lengths to extract the relevant keys from the CA.
  • Whoever has the credentials to the CA account is unknown. It could be the owner, an IT vendor or a government.
  • INR managers in large organizations often have no authority beyond INR registration, such as for bank transactions or server access.
  • Holders change over time. A resource may be held by one party when a document is signed and by another later, or be moved from one CA to another, likely requiring a change of keys.
  • Ghostbuster Records (RFC 6493) are arbitrary and are only clues for operational support contacts; they do not attest to holding any INRs.
  • Proof of possession of a private key does not make someone a valid legal representative of the organization.

Autonomous System Numbers are only identifiers used for loop detection in routing, with no inherent semantics other than uniqueness.
sections.plainLanguage: The key often sits with a middleman, people change jobs, and companies change hands. So holding the key says very little about who is really behind a signature.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using RPKI data to authenticate real-world documents or other artifacts requiring identity may be cryptographically valid within the RPKI, but it is misleading about authenticity.

When a document is signed with the private key of an RPKI certificate, the signer is speaking for the INRs in the certificate. That is an authorization, not an identity. In schemes like Resource Tagged Attestations and Signed Checklists, the signed message narrows the scope further, so its INRs are a subset of those in the certificate. A valid signature means the content comes from a party authorized to speak for that subset.

Control of INRs could also be used to falsely authorize transactions or documents for which the INR manager has no authority. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: A valid signature only says 'this person may speak for these addresses'. Trusting it for anything else could let the wrong person approve things they should not.
